title: Gateless Barrier, Case 1: Zhaozhou's Mu
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 1 of the Gateless Barrier, in which a monk asks Zhaozhou whether a dog has Buddha nature and Zhaozhou answers "Mu." Nomon reads that answer as a "no" meaning "don't be so sure," and offers two zazen practices: breathing out the sound Mu, or breathing into the question "What is it?" Wu Men's commentary follows, with its red-hot iron ball and eyebrows entangled with the ancestors, and Nomon points to the love and joy running through its gnarly language. Nomon also weighs the value of intensity against the extra tension that comes from trying too hard. Nomon closes by holding up calligraphy of the character mu in block, semi-cursive, and grass script styles, including copies of versions by Kaz Tanahashi and Akiba Roshi.

sentences.text: A special transmission outside the scriptures, not depending on words and letters.
It's all a little ironic.
This is part of a vast literature full of words and letters, but it's also very true.
There's an attempt being made here to point to or bring forward a certain kind of freshness, a certain kind of directness, something that's beyond explanation, beyond concept.
But the only tools we have to do this are words and letters, so that's what we've got.
And by the way, these exchanges that eventually became these Zen stories, these Zen koans, in some cases probably derived from a kind of drinking game of the literati.

They would sit around drinking whatever the Chinese version of sake was, quoting poems back and forth with each other and making witty comments, trying to meet one witty comment with another, with lots of references to earlier poems and comments.
It was a very intellectual thing that got stripped down in some way by the Zen people.
Theirs were a little less flowery.
Some of the stories are very short and some are longer.
The first story, Case One in the Mumonkan, is a very short story.
Like many of them, it's an exchange between a student and a master, and the master is named, but not the student.
*A monk asked Master Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha nature or not?"
Zhaozhou said, "Mu."*
He said that.
This is an interesting exchange because in a literal way, it's wrong.
And this, by the way, is the most famous of the Zen koans, studied and commented on endlessly, this little exchange.
Does a dog have Buddha nature or not?
Nope.
Or maybe the best way to say it in English vernacular would be "not."
Pretty much like that: not.
It's not exactly "no, I don't think so," or "no," but it's like "not," mu.
This is literally wrong because in Mahayana Buddhism we have a very strong, central idea that everything is an expression of Buddha nature.
Everything is or has Buddha nature.
And Dogen famously, instead of saying things have Buddha nature, said things are Buddha nature.
We are Buddha.
We are something bigger than we think we are.
We are awake.
We are interconnected and interdependent.
Everything reflects the whole universe in a wondrous way.
So of course dogs have Buddha nature.
There's a lot of use of negation in Zen.
Perhaps you noticed negation in the Heart Sutra that we chanted a little while ago.
No this, no that, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no.
So why do they talk about it that way?
What's the point of all this "no, no, no" in Zen?
The thing is, it's not "no" in opposition to "yes."
It's more like "no" in opposition to being so sure about yes and no.
So sure that there's always a this or that, a big or a small, a black or a white, a yes or a no.
Our deeply held tendency to sort and compare and divide things in that way diminishes and limits the possibility of being a human being who is in fact Buddha, who is Buddha nature.
So it's not a "no" like "no," but a "no" of possibility, a "no" of going beyond, a "no" of boundlessness.
If it's not this and it's not that, then it could be anything.
It could be beyond anything.
So Zhaozhou's Moo here, Zhaozhou's "no," is kind of the "no" of "don't be so sure."

I think this is a wonderful thing that we can really study and use in our lives and offer to the world in the best, most appropriate and helpful ways that we can, because there is so much suffering in the world.

The political sphere is such a clear example these days of the incredible suffering of everyone being so sure of everything, these different surenesses colliding and combating each other and ramming into each other.
This is the "not so sure" of not knowing, of releasing ourselves from the limitation and the narrowness of having a view.
Buddha was very big in the early teachings in warning us not to have fixed views.
It's natural that views arise, but we should recognize they're just views.
They're views that appear based on conditions, based on history and culture and based on everything.
It's just a view.
Moo: don't be so sure of your view.

And this sound Moo is taken up in Zazen in the Rinzai koan study tradition, not as likely as a word, but more like a tone poem to this openness, this boundlessness, this endlessness, that you breathe: Moo.
You can try this in your Zazen.
It would be wonderful, I think, to do this for a while.
To breathe in and really open the space, invite in energy and openness, literally, right?
We breathe in, we're opening.
And breathing out, you could just say to yourself, Moo, just Moo.
And it doesn't need to mean the word "no" or anything.
It's just this sound, this powerful sound.
I've played with this a little bit, and it's interesting and you should play with this, I think.

But without the full structure of that system, of that Zazen koan curriculum, of the teachers talking a lot about this koan, about Moo, and all the students practicing Moo, I haven't found it personally that helpful.
I think it's interesting, but it hasn't really been that transformational for me, to the level that I've been able to engage with Moo.
In those systems, they really get into it, much more than I have.

But what I have found helpful in this space, which was suggested to me by my teacher in our lineage, is practicing with questions in a similar fashion to what I just described about Moo: to breathe in, opening the space, bringing energy into your body, and breathing out to just drop your breath into a question.
It can just be the idea of questioning.
Or a wonderful question to practice with is the question, what is it?
What is it?
So you can breathe in and breathe out: what is it?
What is it?
It's wonderful.
You can establish this in Zazen, what is it?
And after a while these words, "what is it," are like a whole lot of unnecessary sounds, and you just breathe with the feeling of what is it, this kind of non-verbal sound, or just "what?"
You establish this in Zazen and then it becomes available to you as you're walking around and doing your day, at work, moving around, or doing whatever you're doing.
You can really wonder, in a very sincere way: what is it?

This is not like trying to figure out what it is.
Maybe one day in a flash of lightning I'll realize, oh, 32!
Or something like that.
It's more that there's a subtle and incredible quality of engagement and connection that's available.
We just practice with curiosity, with not knowing.
And what better way to not know than to ask yourself an impossible question over and over and over again, with sincerity, with energy?
What is it?
And with this softness and release from outcomes, this letting go of needing to figure something out or have there be an answer.
So a monk asked Master Zhaozhou, does a dog have Buddha nature or not?
What is it?
What is it?
This is interesting if you really commit to it for a while.
I think the most powerful way to take up a practice like this is actually to have it given to you.
You come to Dokusan and we talk about all kinds of things in there, but this is the kind of stuff we're supposed to be talking about, I think.
Zazen.
You can come in and we can talk about your Zazen, with me or one of the other teachers, and if it feels right, it's helpful to receive from your teacher, "Why don't you practice with this question?"
It could be this question or another question.
Then really commit to it and really work with it, and have this accountability of "yeah, come see me later and tell me about it, what's coming up."
It's not like there's exactly an answer.
But it's also really good to practice in a very simple way.
The first practice always is the establishment of stability of mind, a certain grounded kind of awareness and attention.
So maybe if you asked me, I'd say, well, that would be interesting later.
Maybe it's good to just follow your breath, just feel the feeling of the body, just practice being very, very present for a while.
Some years, and then we can play with the question.
That's the traditional thing to do: not to talk about these different practices so much in Dharma talks.

It's also probably most effective to get your marching orders in the Dokusan room and really commit to something for a while and see what happens.
So let's listen a little to Master Wu Men's enthusiastic commentary on this case.
This is very much in the intense and enthusiastic style of the Rinzai Zen school.
The case is just two lines, but the commentary is several paragraphs about how wonderful it is to really get into the practice with Mu.
Excuse me.
*For the practice of Zen, it is imperative that you pass through the barrier set up by the ancestral teachers.
For subtle realization, it is of the utmost importance that you cut off the mind road.
If you do not pass the barriers of the ancestors, if you do not cut off the mind road, then you are a ghost clinging to bushes and grasses.
What is this barrier of the ancestral teachers?
It is just this word, Mu.
The one barrier of our faith.
We call it the gateless barrier of the Zen tradition.
When you pass through this barrier, you will not only interview Zhao Zhou intimately yourself, you will walk hand in hand with all the ancestral teachers in the successive generations of our lineage.
The hair of your eyebrows will be entangled with theirs.*
Is that a cool image?
Entangled with their eyebrow hair.
*And you'll see with the same eyes and hear with the same ears.
Won't that be fulfilling?
Is there anyone who would not want to pass this barrier?*
You on board?
So here's how you do it.
And by the way, Master Wu Men, studying this koan was really big in his practice, so that's why he's so fired up.
He had a big experience with this koan.
Now he's going to give us some directions, and now [unclear: "Harry"] gets very gnarly.
*So, make your whole body a mass of doubt.
And with your 360 bones and joints, and your 84,000 hair follicles, concentrate on this one word, mu.
Day and night.
Keep digging into it.
Don't consider it to be nothingness.
Don't consider it in terms of has and has not.
When you really practice this way, it is like swallowing a red-hot iron ball.
You try to vomit it out, but you can't.
Gradually you purify yourself, eliminating mistaken knowledge and attitudes that you've held from the past.
Inside and outside become one.
You're like a mute person who has had a dream.
You know it for yourself alone.
Suddenly mu breaks open, the heavens are astonished, the earth is shaken.
It is as though you have snatched the great sword of General Quan.
When you meet the Buddha, you kill the Buddha.
When you meet Bodhidharma, you kill Bodhidharma.
At the very cliff edge of birth and death, you find the great freedom.
In the six worlds and the four modes of birth, you enjoy the samadhi of frolic and play.
How then should you work with this?
Exhaust all your life energy on this one word, mu.
If you do not falter, then it's done.
A single spark lights your Dharma candle.*
Just reading that again, I realize it's easy to focus on the red-hot iron ball, the stuff you can't vomit out.
But there's actually a really lovely sense here, isn't there, too, of connection and love.
You walk hand in hand with the ancestral teachers.
Your eyebrows entangled.
You enjoy the frolic and play, in the samadhi of joy.
So there's a lot of love and joy in this, even mixed in with the very gnarly and intense language of traditional Zen.
Not to say that we couldn't do with a little intensity from time to time.
It's good to go for it.
I think it would be a mistake to think this practice is just about sitting on our butts.
When we were talking about this at the sesshin, there's a little danger with us that we just put it in park.
And then eventually somebody rings the bell and we're like, what?
Hi.
I'm still here, I guess.
And yet, the "and yet" is, there's enough suffering already.
We don't have to create more tension and pain by trying too hard.
So there's an interesting balance here to play with.
How can we really be inspired by and guided by these traditional Zen stories and the teachings that rose up around them over the centuries, so that we're really taking this possibility seriously?
The invitation here is complete transformation.
Not just feeling a little better or being a little calmer.
It's actually turning our lives around in a certain way, so we're not caught.
We're not suffering.
So the things that arise don't need to bother us.

Are we so sure of everything?

Not, you know, mu!
